meetings.title: Intercompany Item Mapping
meetings.summary: The group discussed how to represent Interplastic-related items in M3 while avoiding duplicate item numbers across companies and facilities. The preferred model was to keep a single shared item definition where possible, with NAC and Plastic using M3 intercompany functionality to handle transfers and accounting automatically.

detailedSummary.overview: The group discussed how to represent Interplastic-related items in M3 while avoiding duplicate item numbers across companies and facilities. The preferred model was to keep a single shared item definition where possible, with NAC and Plastic using M3 intercompany functionality to handle transfers and accounting automatically.
keyPoints: Interplastic appears to use one item number, with item attributes and classification fields determining how the item is used rather than creating separate numbers by company or facility.
A maintained vendor item cross-reference or item mask was identified as the appropriate M3-supported bridge if different external item references must be connected.
Using the same item master definition enables NAC to submit a distribution order and lets M3 create the intercompany accounting in the background, avoiding manual AP and AR processing.
NAC and Plastic currently classify similar materials differently, including differences between item group and item type usage, which complicates shared item design.
The group noted that some item classification fields drive downstream behavior and may not be changeable after setup, so the item master design needs to be handled carefully.
Past Molding Products cleanup required adoption of Plastic raw material codes where products were truly the same, but did not fully clean up every legacy code.

Customer, supplier, payer, ship-to, and deliver-from structures have similar ownership ambiguity: a payer or supplier number alone does not reliably identify the business unit without additional context.
Future reporting or gold model design will likely need ERD-style relationships, with some dimensions shared across domains and some relationships modeled as one-way rather than bidirectional.
actionItems: Confirm whether a maintained vendor item cross-reference or item mask exists for the item and use that as the only mapping bridge if needed.
Validate the NAC-master / Plastic-receiving model against the actual M3 intercompany distribution order and accounting flow.
Identify which item master classification fields drive downstream behavior and which cannot be changed after setup.
Align with business stakeholders on whether the item should remain one shared definition across facilities and companies.
Model the customer, supplier, payer, ship-to, deliver-from, and warehouse-item relationships clearly for future reporting or gold model design.

meetings.title: Monthly IT All Hands
meetings.summary: The meeting focused on confirming how Power BI reports connect to warehouse data and how that should translate into a governed gold-model architecture by domain. The team aligned that live/direct-connected reports should filter and secure data in the Power BI semantic model, while upstream source mapping is needed before locking the first domain model.

detailedSummary.overview: The meeting focused on confirming how Power BI reports connect to warehouse data and how that should translate into a governed gold-model architecture by domain. The team aligned that live/direct-connected reports should filter and secure data in the Power BI semantic model, while upstream source mapping is needed before locking the first domain model.
keyPoints: Michelle is the known user of the report discussed at the start of the session.
The report appears to use a live/direct connection to the warehouse, which means the report updates as soon as source data lands and does not rely on scheduled refresh.
Because direct/live connections do not support Power Query transformation steps in the same way, filtering should happen in Power BI through DAX, report filters, and model-level rules.
The intended pattern is one governed gold model per domain that contains the facts, dimensions, joins, and row-level security rules needed by that domain’s reports.
Report builders should connect to the domain gold model rather than creating separate datasets or reaching around it to one-off sources.
If a report needs data that is missing from the gold model, the requirement should be escalated so the data engineering team can add it to the model.
The first domain onboarding step is to inventory all reports and source tables, then identify the tables that provide broad coverage across the domain.

Speaker 4’s execution package includes templates and worksheets for usage summaries, artifact inventory, governance, implementation playbooks, domain documentation, data contracts, architecture diagrams, workshops, and presentations.
actionItems: Retrieve Speaker 4’s execution package from the shared location and identify the worksheet/tab listing upstream source tables, downstream reports, governance, and ownership.
Confirm which domain will be onboarded first; customer was used as the working example but still needs formal confirmation.
Map the exact Power BI dataset name for the report in scope and identify whether it reads from a view or directly from warehouse tables.
Determine whether Michelle’s report is connected to an existing view, a gold table, or a lower-level warehouse table.
Document the initial gold model shape for the chosen domain, including core fact table, shared dimensions, joins, and model-level RLS rules.
Circulate the Kimball Data Warehouse Toolkit and Data Warehouse Lifecycle Toolkit to the team, with at least the first chapter recommended before proceeding.

actionItems: Here is the prep package for this upcoming meeting....--- tags: - all --- # Meeting Prep — Historian Data Extraction Update (this week, 2026-05-19 to 23) > Audience: Steve + Patrick (pre-align). Internal voice — candid, direct. > Origin: Jim Cecere's follow-up request, continuing from Patrick's 2026-04-07 email reframing the extraction owner as Robert/Ryan. > Teams link: https://teams.microsoft.com/meet/21208845130301?p=8e92WNSACwr2sbKloW · Meeting ID 212 088 451 303 01 · Passcode `ia9QS3A4` --- ## 1. Why this meeting exists Jim Cecere (VP R&D) called the follow-up to figure out the **data we want, who pulls it, and how Citrine ingests it**. Patrick's 2026-04-07 note already drew the line: this is a one-time controls/historian extract, so **Robert LaMontagne or Ryan Mozzetti** owns the pull; Jim's R&D team owns what to ask for; Citrine validates the sample format/volume; Steve + Patrick own the long-term Fabric trajectory. The job in this meeting isn't to design Fabric Bronze for the historian — it's to **finalize the sample extract** and **un-stick the four-week silence** since the last on-the-record session (2026-04-10). The 2026-04-30 continuation has no transcript and produced no captured decisions, so we're effectively walking in cold on status. ## 2. Where things stand (with citations) ### Last confirmed status — 2026-04-10 Historian Data Extraction session Captured in [`meetings/summaries/2026-04-10-historian-data-extraction.md`](../../meetings/summaries/2026-04-10-historian-data-extraction.md) (full Teams transcript): - Historian data extraction is **manual, batch-by-batch** today; no automated pull exists. - Robert estimated **~3 months** for "initial data loading"; Patrick said full implementation would be longer, contingent on approvals. - **Phase interval batch data** should be available; Ryan was assigned to contact **Tony** for access or adjustments. - Mark Sullivan (Citrine), Ryan, Robert reviewed the **Citrine data framework** — which batch-level single-point values to extract, distinguishing inputs vs. outputs. Expert input was flagged as critical for variable selection. - Robert took the action to **reach out to Cybertrol (Cyber Control)** for an extract, keeping Patrick and Steve in the loop. - Robert was to contact **Tim** for database differences across sites and **Sabichal** for the Prior-site report. - Robert was to reach out to **Matt Finch** for fabric-upgrade approval (per Patrick). - Group agreed to reconvene in two weeks → that became the 2026-04-30 session. ### What we DON'T have — 2026-04-30 continuation [`meetings/summaries/2026-04-30-historian-data-extraction-cont.md`](../../meetings/summaries/2026-04-30-historian-data-extraction-cont.md) is a STUB. Calendar metadata only — Patrick, Mozzetti, Robert, Hackman, Sullivan, Mathers, Grove. No transcript. **We don't know what was decided.** Treat this as Open Question #1 in the meeting: "Robert / Pat, can you catch us up on what came out of the 30th — I don't have notes from that one." ### Patrick's 2026-04-07 role split (the doctrine for this meeting) > *"Since this is a one-time extract within the controls/historian domain, Robert or Ryan should take charge of this extraction process… The immediate priority is to deliver a sample extract for Citrine to validate format, volume, and ingestion requirements… The long-term goal will be moving this data into Fabric, which will still require additional coordination with Robert."* Translation: - **Robert / Ryan**: own the extract. - **Citrine team** (Mark Sullivan + Alicia Andrews-Vafai / Anne Hackman): validate format/volume/ingestion once the sample lands. - **Jim Cecere**: owns the R&D-side "what do we want?" — the variable selection from the 04-10 framework discussion. - **Steve + Patrick**: own the Fabric trajectory and the network/security plumbing. ### Citrine context refresher From [`project-memory/systems-landscape.md`](../../project-memory/systems-landscape.md) (Citrine entry): - Cloud-based materials-informatics / AI property-prediction platform from **Citrine Informatics**. - Primary data source today is **Optiva** (PLM formulas, ingredients, raw-material specs) via SQL export. - Historian feeds the **process-data** side of the picture that Citrine doesn't have yet — temperatures, viscosity curves, AV trajectories, hold times. - SAML SSO already wired up week of 2026-01-09. Mark Sullivan is the Citrine PM; Alicia Andrews-Vafai / Anne Hackman are the materials-informatics engineers on Citrine's side. - Known integration gotcha from 2026-04-30 Citrine working session: **`levels` parameter silent-failure** in the Citrine Excel ingest tool — if set too shallow, you miss recursive children (Alkyd batches case). Don't accept "looks fine" without verifying every batch type is represented. ### What the Plant Tour (yesterday, 2026-05-19) adds From [`meetings/summaries/2026-05-19-plant-tour.md`](../../meetings/summaries/2026-05-19-plant-tour.md), three things land directly on this meeting: - **Viscometer auto-populates MES; AV (acid value) is manual entry.** That means for any batch-level extract for Citrine, the curve points are MES-resident, but anything AV-dependent has manual-entry timestamp gaps to be aware of. (`DISC-2026-05-19-017`) - **Pilot reactor batches aren't in MES at all.** Andre creates batch numbers manually. (`DISC-2026-05-19-009`). If R&D wants pilot-scale process data in Citrine, the data isn't reachable from the historian/MES stack alone. - **Total Automation Project completed ~18 months ago** — the historian-adjacent PLC layer is current-generation; we're not dealing with a 30-year-old system. (`DISC-2026-05-19-016`) ### Today's separate Preface Fabric Meeting context (2026-05-19) Not central to this meeting, but worth carrying in your back pocket: see [`meetings/summaries/2026-05-19-preface-fabric-meeting.md`](../../meetings/summaries/2026-05-19-preface-fabric-meeting.md) — the M3 Cloud → Fabric path and the SQL Server mirroring conversation are the **same architectural pattern** we'll eventually want for the historian. If Jim or Robert asks "what happens after the sample?" the answer is **Fabric Bronze via mirroring or a direct pull, parallel to what we just scoped for SQL Server sources** — not a new bespoke pipeline. ## 3. Attendees + signals | Person | Role | What they'll likely push for | Signal to watch for | |---|---|---|---| | **Jim Cecere** | VP R&D, Interplastic | A concrete timeline for getting Citrine *useful data* — he's the demand pull. May press on "is this sample going to be enough or do we need more?" | Frustration with extraction taking longer than R&D feels it should. He's the one with the budget at stake. | | **Patrick Stiller** | IT Manager, our day-to-day | Keep the controls/historian work with Robert/Ryan; protect Steve's bandwidth for Fabric/governance. May echo "this is a one-time thing." | If Patrick wants to pull back from Cybertrol coordination, that's a flag we should catch. | | **Robert LaMontagne** | OT Contact / Process Control Manager | Owns the actual extract. Will report on Cybertrol outreach, Tony/Tim/Sabichal status. | If he hedges on the 3-month estimate from 04-10, that's the real news. | | **Ryan Mozzetti** | Controls engineer (assumed — no stakeholder-map entry yet — see Open Question below) | Tactical execution — what comes out of the historian, in what shape. | If Ryan got blocked on Tony or on phase-interval data, surface it. | | **Steve (you)** | Architect / Fabric owner | Connect the sample-extract work to the Fabric Bronze trajectory without taking the extraction work back onto your plate. | Don't accidentally re-own the extract. Robert/Ryan lead. | **Likely also in the room** (from the recurring Historian working group + Citrine cadence): Mark Sullivan, Bradley Grove, Dominique Mathers, possibly Anne Hackman. Calendar will confirm. ## 4. Your goal for the meeting > **Walk out with a named sample extract spec, a named owner, and a target date.** Everything else is bonus. A "sample extract spec" means: which **tags / variables**, for which **batch types**, over what **time window**, in what **file format**, delivered to **whom**. If we leave without those five things named, the next meeting is a re-run. Secondary goal: **set up the long-term Fabric ingestion conversation as a follow-up**, not in this meeting. Avoid letting the discussion balloon into "and then how do we Fabric." Anchor that as a Patrick-and-Steve follow-up. ## 5. Talking points (in order) 1. **Opener (≤ 90 seconds):** "Jim, thanks for setting this up. Quick frame — the 4-10 session put the framework on the table and the 4-30 continuation got into more detail. I want to use today to lock the sample extract scope and the timeline, then keep the long-term Fabric path as a separate Patrick-and-me follow-up." 2. **Status check (pull from Robert):** "Robert, can you catch us up since the 30th? Where did the Cybertrol outreach land? Did we hear back on phase-interval data from Tony, and on the site differences from Tim?" *(Why this matters: we have no transcript from 4-30 in the brain. This question fills the gap and gets the room oriented.)* 3. **Citrine validation framing:** "Mark / Anne — Patrick's 4-7 note set the priority as a **sample** that Citrine validates for format, volume, and ingestion. What's the minimum sample size that lets you tell us whether the shape works? And is there anything beyond batch-level single-point values you need to see to give us a clean yes/no?" 4. **The five-thing spec:** Walk the room through the five things we need to leave with: - **Variables / tags** — the input/output list from the 04-10 framework discussion. Has Mark + Ryan + Robert finalized it? - **Batch types** — every type that matters, including (deliberately) at least one Alkyd batch, given the levels-parameter silent-failure we hit on 04-30 in the Citrine working session. - **Time window** — how far back, how many batches, calendar window or batch-count. - **Format** — what file type Citrine prefers for sample ingest (CSV / parquet / Excel via their tool). - **Delivery target** — secure transfer mechanism + named recipient on Citrine's side. 5. **Fabric trajectory framing (one minute, no longer):** "On the long-term — once we have a working sample, Patrick and I will design the Bronze ingestion path. It'll likely parallel what we're now scoping for SQL Server sources via Fabric mirroring. I'll come back to this group with that plan; it doesn't need to slow down the sample work." 6. **Close — confirm next steps + owner + date:** Read them back. Robert / Ryan: extraction owner. Date: explicit. Mark / Anne: validation owner. Next meeting: when. ## 6. Questions to ask (in priority order) 1. **Robert:** What came out of the 30th — what's the current status of the Cybertrol outreach for the extract? 2. **Robert / Ryan:** Did Tony come through on phase-interval data access? If not, where's it stuck? 3. **Robert:** Status on Tim (site DB differences) and Sabichal (Prior site report) — those were open from 04-10. 4. **Robert:** Did Matt Finch sign off on the fabric upgrade approval you were going to ask him about? 5. **Mark / Anne (Citrine):** Minimum viable sample for you to give a thumbs-up on format/volume? What's the worst-case "this sample doesn't tell us enough" answer look like? 6. **Ryan / Mark:** Has the input vs. output variable list been finalized since 04-10? If yes, where's it documented? 7. **Jim:** Is there a hard date — internal R&D milestone, board commitment, anything — driving urgency on the Citrine side that we should be aware of? 8. **Patrick:** Do we need to formalize the Cybertrol scope under SOW W34130 or is this a small-enough one-time pull that an email suffices? ## 7. Things to NOT promise / red lines - **Don't take ownership of the extract.** Robert / Ryan own it per Patrick's 4-7 doctrine. If pressure builds for you to "just do it," push back: the controls/historian domain is theirs. - **Don't commit to a Fabric Bronze production date** for historian data. The Fabric historian Bronze design is a *separate* downstream thread that happens after the sample-validate handshake; it's not on the table today. - **Don't accept "we'll figure out the variables later"** — that's how we end up rerunning the 04-10 framework conversation in 6 weeks. Push for a named list out of today. - **Don't accept "the extract is fine, looks good"** without an explicit Alkyd-batch check (per the 04-30 Citrine session silent-failure pattern with the `levels` parameter). - **Don't agree to add the historian to the weekly MDM status email scope** — keep it separate as a controls/historian extract until it actually becomes part of the Fabric program. ## 8. Autonomy progresses from Day 1 recommendations to Week 2 pattern learning, Month 3 bundled approvals, and Year 1 autonomous execution for low-risk work.
The product philosophy is restraint: Natively stays light and calm because the brain carries the system's intelligence burden.
